On a particular specialization of monomial symmetric functions

Vincent Brugidoua00footnotetext: E-mail address vincent.brugidou@univ-lille.fr

a Université de Lille, 59655 Villeneuve d’Ascq cedex, France

Abstract : Let mλm_{\lambda} be the monomial symmetric functions, λ\lambda being an integer partition of n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast}. For the specialization corresponding to the qq-deformation of the exponential, we prove that each mλm_{\lambda} is associated with a polynomial Jλ​(q)J_{\lambda}\left(q\right) whose coefficients belong to ℤ\mathbb{Z}. JλJ_{\lambda} is an algebraic generalization of the case λ=(n)\lambda=\left(n\right) for which J(n)=JnJ_{\left(n\right)}=J_{n} is the enumerator of tree inversions. We establish several relations between JλJ_{\lambda} and the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}, which were defined algebraically in our previous work for n≥r≥1n\geq r\geq 1, and are classical combinatorial enumerators with Jn(1)=JnJ_{n}^{\left(1\right)}=J_{n}. Based on inductive computations of JλJ_{\lambda} for n≤43n\leq 43, we conjecture that the coefficients of each JλJ_{\lambda} are strictly positive and log-concave. As a consequence of Huh’s Theorem on the hh-vector of matroid complex, it is shown that the coefficients of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} are strictly positive and log-concave, which gives a second argument in favor of these conjectures. Furthermore, we prove that the last n−1n-1 coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are proportional to the first coefficients of the (n−r−1n-r-1)-th column of Pascal’s triangle, where rr is the length of λ\lambda. This is a third argument in favor of the conjectures. However, The calculation of J(3,2,1)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)} reveals a difficulty, if one wishes to prove the conjectures through the application of Huh’s theorem mentioned above.

keywords : monomial symmetric functions, q-deformation of the exponential, tree inversions, log-concavity, hh-vector of matroids.

1 Introduction

Let pn(r)p_{n}^{\left(r\right)} be the symmetric functions defined for any pair of integers (n,r)\left(n,r\right) such that n≥r≥1n\geq r\geq 1, by

pn(r)=∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=rmλ​,p_{n}^{(r)}=\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}m_{\lambda}\text{,} (1.1)

where mλ m_{\lambda\text{ }} are the monomial symmetric functions and the sum is taking over all integer partitions λ\lambda of nn of length l⁡(λ)=rl(\lambda)=r. The functions pn(r)p_{n}^{(r)} are introduced with this notation in [12​, Example 19, p. 33]\left[12\text{, Example 19, p. 33}\right]. In particular, pn(1)p_{n}^{\left(1\right)} is the power symetric function pn=mnp_{n}=m_{n}. In [8], we showed the following result for the specialization whose generating function of elementary symmetric function is given by the following Equation (1.2)\left(1.2\right), sometimes called the qq-deformation of the exponential.

Theorem 6.3 i) of [8]\left[8\right] For n≥r≥1n\geq r\geq 1, and the specialization

Ex​q​(t)=∑n=0∞q(n2)​tnn!​,E_{xq}(t)=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}q^{\binom{n}{2}}\dfrac{t^{n}}{n!}\text{,} (1.2)

we have :

pn(r)=(1−q)n−r​q(r2)r!​(n−r)!​Jn(r)​(q)​,p_{n}^{(r)}=\left(1-q\right)^{n-r}\dfrac{q^{\binom{r}{2}}}{r!\left(n-r\right)!}J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}(q)\text{,} (1.3)

where Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} is a monic polynomial with positive integer coefficients, whose constant term is (n−r)!\left(n-r\right)! and whose degree is (n−12)−(r−12)\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2}. Moreover, for all r≥1r\geq 1, Jr(r)=1J_{r}^{\left(r\right)}=1.

When r=1r=1, this gives

mn=pn=pn(1)=(1−q)n−1(n−1)!​Jn​,m_{n}=p_{n}=p_{n}^{\left(1\right)}=\dfrac{\left(1-q\right)^{n-1}}{\left(n-1\right)!}J_{n}\text{,} (1.4)

where Jn=Jn(1)J_{n}=J_{n}^{\left(1\right)} is the enumerator polynomial of inversions in trees on nn vertices, introduced in [13]. More generally, the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} enumerate inversions for sequences for sequences of ”colored” forests introduced by Stanley and Yan (see [18]\left[18\right] and [19]\left[19\right]), or level statistic enumerators introduced in Section 9 of [8]\left[8\right]. Alternatively, the reciprocal polynomial of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}, denoted Jn(r)¯\overline{J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}} in [8]\left[8\right], is the sum enumerator of generalized parking functions. We refer to the survey [20] and to [8]\left[8\right] for more details on these combinatorial representations.

When we take λ\lambda to be the partition (n)\left(n\right), the monomial mλm_{\lambda} factors as in (1.4)\left(1.4\right) for the specialization (1.2)\left(1.2\right). The question that motivated our work is wether a similar factorization exists for any partition λ\lambda. The answer is affirmative and is given by Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.5. The factorization of mλm_{\lambda} yields a polynomial JλJ_{\lambda} whose coefficients belong to ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and which algebraically generalizes JnJ_{n}. This is proven by induction using two order relations on the set of integer partitions. It follows two recurrence relations allowing all JλJ_{\lambda} to be calculated from the initial condition J1=1J_{1}=1 (Corollary 3.7). In Section 4, based on the computations of JλJ_{\lambda} for n=|λ|≤43n=\left|\lambda\right|\leq 43, we conjecture that, for any partition λ\lambda, the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are positive and log-concave. A second argument supporting these conjectures is that we show (Proposition 4.4) the log-concavity of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} using Huh’s results on the hh-vector of the matroid complex of representable matroids over a field of characteristic zero. We also prove in Section 5 that the last n−1n-1 coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are proportional to the first n−1n-1 coefficients of the (n−r−1n-r-1)-th column of Pascal’s triangle. This provides a third argument in favor of the conjectures since it is well known that these columns are log-concave. To conclude, in Section 6 we discuss various approaches to fully prove the conjectures.

4 Conjectures about JλJ_{\lambda}

Three heuristic arguments lead us to state the following conjectures.

Conjecture 4.1

For any partition λ\lambda the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are strictly positive.

To state the second and third conjectures, let us recall some definitions. If a=(ak)0≤k≤na=\left(a_{k}\right)_{0\leq k\leq n} is a finite sequence of real numbers, then :

* aa is unimodal if there is an index jj, 0≤j≤n0\leq j\leq n such that

a0≤a1≤…≤aj−1≤aj≥aj+1≥…≥an​.a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq...\leq a_{j-1}\leq a_{j}\geq a_{j+1}\geq...\geq a_{n}\text{.}

* aa is log-concave (resp. strictly log-concave) if

aj2≥aj−1​aj+1​(resp.​aj2>aj−1​aj+1)for all​ 1≤j≤n−1​.a_{j}^{2}\geq a_{j-1}a_{j+1}\ (\text{resp.}\;a_{j}^{2}>a_{j-1}a_{j+1})\ \ \text{for all}\ 1\leq j\leq n-1\text{.}

* aa has no internal zeros if there do not exist i<j<ki<j<k satisfying ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0, aj=0a_{j}=0 and ak≠0a_{k}\neq 0.

We will also say that the polynomial Pa​(q)=a0+a1​q+…+an​qnP_{a}\left(q\right)=a_{0}+a_{1}q+...+a_{n}q^{n} has one of these properties if the sequence of its coefficients owns it. More details on theses properties and a rich variety of unimodal and log-concave sequences can be found in [5​, ​7​, ​17]\left[5\text{, }7\text{, }17\right].

Conjecture 4.2

For any partition λ\lambda, JλJ_{\lambda} is log-concave.

If these two conjectures are true then JλJ_{\lambda} is also unimodal (see Lemma 7.1.1 of [5]\left[5\right]), thus we can also state :

Conjecture 4.3

For any partition λ\lambda, JλJ_{\lambda} is unimodal.

Let us note that it is equivalent to formulate these conjectures for the polynomials JλJ_{\lambda}, MλM_{\lambda} or J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda}=Jλ/ΔJ_{\lambda}/\Delta, where Δ\Delta is the GCD of the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda}. The first argument supporting the statement of these conjectures comes from the computations already performed. On the one hand, the conjectures are obviously true for J1nJ_{1^{n}} and J1n−2​2J_{1^{n-2}2} given by Equations (3.21)\left(3.21\right) and (3.22)\left(3.22\right). On the other hand, by developing a program based on Corollary 3.73.7, Dr. Philippe Bodart of the University of Lille, computed the polynomials JλJ_{\lambda} and verified the conjectures for |λ|=n≤43\left|\lambda\right|=n\leq 43. Given the exponential growth in the number of integer partitions of nn, this represents 376325 polynomials. In other words, for each of these polynomials, the strict positivity and log-concavity of their coefficients were verified. Note that the highest degree among these polynomials is 861, which correspond to the cases of J43J_{43} and J(42,1)J_{\left(42,1\right)}, as one can calculate using Corollary 3.5.

The second argument in favor of these conjectures comes from the fact that the coefficients of the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} are strictly positive and log-concave, as we will demonstrate below. This follow from Huh’s work and is actually true for a broader class of polynomials denoted Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} in [20]\left[20\right] ( Do not confuse the aa of Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} with the sequence a=(ak)0≤k≤na=\left(a_{k}\right)_{0\leq k\leq n} above). We saw in ([8]\left[8\right], Section 6) that these polynomials are related to Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} through the relation Jn(r)=In−r(r​,1)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=I_{n-r}^{\left(r,1\right)}. The polynomials Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} and their reciprocals, which are the sum enumerators of the generalized classical parking functions, have been the subject of extensive research, a summary of which can be found in [20].

i) The sequence of the coefficients of each polynomial Im(a,b)I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)} is strictly positive and log-concave, thus unimodal.

where Tn/rT_{n/r} is the Tutte polynomial of a graph which we denote Kn/rK_{n/r} : Kn/rK_{n/r} is the complete graph KnK_{n} in which all edges between rr given vertices are contracted.

Im(a,b)​(q)=∑i=cdai​qi​.I_{m}^{\left(a,b\right)}\left(q\right)=\sum\limits_{i=c}^{d}a_{i}q^{i}\text{.}

ii) First, note that the contracted graph Kn/rK_{n/r} clearly does not depend on the choice of rr vertices (see [9]\left[9\right] for an illustration). Let KnK_{n} be the complete graph on nn vertices, and let RR be any set of rr vertices among these nn vertices. Contract all the edges between the rr vertices of RR, and number 00 the vertex that replaces these rr vertices. The set of other vertices 𝐧−R\mathbf{n}-R, and the edges between these vertices, remain unchanged in the contraction. In the contracted graph, denoted Kn/rK_{n/r}, there is thus one edge between two vertices of 𝐧−R\mathbf{n}-R, and rr edges between a vertex of 𝐧−R\mathbf{n}-R and vertex 00. This shows that Kn/rK_{n/r} is isomorphic to Kn−r+11,rK_{n-r+1}^{1,r} and proves Equation (4.1)\left(4.1\right) as a special case of (4.5)\left(4.5\right).  

Remark 4.5

Kn(r)K_{n}^{\left(r\right)} would be a more coherent notation to designate the contracted graph of 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii) but this notation is already used for the complete rr-uniform hypergraph of order nn, see [4, p. 310]. To our knowledge, there is no simple standard notation assigned to the considered family of graph. The proposed notation Kn/rK_{n/r} is quite suggestive, even if it is not entirely satisfactory because a contraction is normally done on edges and not on vertices.

We have just proven that the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}, and in particular Jn=Jn(1)J_{n}=J_{n}^{\left(1\right)}, verify the conjectures. Moreover, there are close links between the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} and JλJ_{\lambda}. Firstly, they have a non-empy intersection corresponding to the three sequences of polynomials extracted from JλJ_{\lambda}, i.e., for λ=(n)\lambda=\left(n\right) as seen before, and for λ=\lambda= 1n1^{n} and 1n−2​211^{n-2}2^{1} as shown by Equations (3.21)\left(3.21\right) and (3.22)\left(3.22\right), respectively. Furthermore, Equations (3.19)\left(3.19\right) and (3.20)\left(3.20\right) are equations relating the JλJ_{\lambda} to the Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} with coefficients that are polynomials in qq with strictly positive integer coefficients. All these facts constitute the second argument in favor of the conjectures. We now present the third argument.

Theorem 5.1 shows that the n−1n-1 coefficients of ((n−1)!/(r−1)!)​Mλ\left(\left(n-1\right)!/(r-1)!\right)M_{\lambda} with highest degree are given by the first n−1n-1 coefficients of column (n−r−1)\left(n-r-1\right) in Pascal’s triangle. Pn(r)P_{n}^{\left(r\right)} and it coefficients will be called Pascalian part and Pascalian coefficients of MλM_{\lambda} (likewise for the parts and coefficients corresponding to JλJ_{\lambda} and J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda}).

Proof. We prove it by a double induction on nn and rr.

a) If n=2n=2 and r=1r=1, we clearly have M(2)=J2=1M_{\left(2\right)}=J_{2}=1 and n⁡((2))=d⁡((2))=0n\left(\left(2\right)\right)=d\left(\left(2\right)\right)=0. Thus the assertion of Theorem 5.1 is true for n=n= |λ|=2\left|\lambda\right|=2 and λ≠12\lambda\neq 1^{2}.

b) Suppose that for k≤nk\leq n, |λ|=k\left|\lambda\right|=k and λ≠1k\lambda\neq 1^{k} the assertion of Theorem 5.1 is true. For λ=(n+1)\lambda=\left(n+1\right), (3.15)\left(3.15\right) gives

M(n+1)=∑r=1n∑|λ|=n​l​(λ)=rMλm⁡(λ)!​.M_{\left(n+1\right)}=\sum\limits_{r=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{M_{\lambda}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}\text{.} (5.3)

For λ\lambda such that |λ|=n\left|\lambda\right|=n and different from 1n1^{n}, we have r≤n−1r\leq n-1, so (5.1)\left(5.1\right) gives

v⁡(λ)=d⁡(λ)−n+2=(n−12)+r−(n−1)≤(n−12)=v⁡((n+1))​.v\left(\lambda\right)=d\left(\lambda\right)-n+2=\binom{n-1}{2}+r-\left(n-1\right)\leq\binom{n-1}{2}=v\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)\text{.}

Therefore, in the sum deduced from (5.3)\left(5.3\right) which gives the coefficient of qmq^{m} in M(n+1)M_{\left(n+1\right)}, all coefficients ⟨qm⟩​Mλ\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\lambda} for λ≠1n\lambda\neq 1^{n} are Pascalian provided that m≥v⁡((n+1))m\geq v\left(\left(n+1\right)\right). We saw that

M1nn!=m~1nn!=q(n2)n!​,\dfrac{M_{1^{n}}}{n!}=\dfrac{\widetilde{m}_{1^{n}}}{n!}=\dfrac{q^{\binom{n}{2}}}{n!}\text{,}

and according to (3.3)\left(3.3\right), d⁡((n+1))=(n2)d\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)=\binom{n}{2}. Thus for v⁡((n+1))≤m≤d⁡((n+1))−1v\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)\leq m\leq d\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)-1, the terms of the sum in (5.3)\left(5.3\right) which contribute to ⟨qm⟩​M(n+1)\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\left(n+1\right)} are the terms associated with the partitions verifying d⁡(λ)≥md\left(\lambda\right)\geq m, i.e. with (3.3)\left(3.3\right), r=l⁡(λ)≥m+1−(n−12)r=l\left(\lambda\right)\geq m+1-\binom{n-1}{2}. By (5.2)\left(5.2\right) and d⁡(λ)−i=m⇔i=d⁡(λ)−md\left(\lambda\right)-i=m\Leftrightarrow i=d\left(\lambda\right)-m, it follows that

⟨qm⟩​Mλ=(r−1)!(n−1)!​(n−r−1+d⁡(λ)−md⁡(λ)−m)​,\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\lambda}=\dfrac{\left(r-1\right)!}{\left(n-1\right)!}\binom{n-r-1+d\left(\lambda\right)-m}{d(\lambda)-m}\text{,}

by adding these expressions, this gives

⟨qm⟩​M(n+1)=∑r=m+1−(n−12)n(r−1)!(n−1)!​∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r(n−r−1+d⁡(λ)−md⁡(λ)−m)m⁡(λ)!​.\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\left(n+1\right)}=\sum\limits_{r=m+1-\binom{n-1}{2}}^{n}\dfrac{\left(r-1\right)!}{\left(n-1\right)!}\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{\binom{n-r-1+d\left(\lambda\right)-m}{d(\lambda)-m}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}\text{.}

Let m=v⁡((n+1))+jm=v\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)+j, substituting mm in the above equation, we obtain for 0≤j≤n−20\leq j\leq n-2 :

⟨qv⁡((n+1))+j⟩​M(n+1)=∑r=j+1n(r−1)!(n−1)!​(n−2+jr−1−j)​∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r1m⁡(λ)!​.\left\langle q^{v\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)+j}\right\rangle M_{\left(n+1\right)}=\sum\limits_{r=j+1}^{n}\dfrac{\left(r-1\right)!}{\left(n-1\right)!}\binom{n-2+j}{r-1-j}\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{1}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}\text{.} (5.4)

Furthermore, it is known that

∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r1m⁡(λ)!=(n!)−1​Bn,r​(1!​,2!,…)=(n−1r−1)​1r!​,\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{1}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}=\left(n!\right)^{-1}B_{n,r}\left(1!,2!,...\right)=\binom{n-1}{r-1}\dfrac{1}{r!}\text{,} (5.5)

where Bn,r​(x1,x2,…)B_{n,r}\left(x_{1},x_{2},...\right) is the Bell’s partial exponential polynomial, the last equality coming from equation [3​h]\left[3h\right] p.135 of [10]\left[10\right]. Using Chu-Vandermonde’s identity given by (see Formula [13​c′]\left[13c^{\prime}\right] p. 44 of [10]\left[10\right]) :

∑l=0L(Al)​(BL−l)=(A+BL)​,\sum\limits_{l=0}^{L}\binom{A}{l}\binom{B}{L-l}=\binom{A+B}{L}\text{,}

we finally obtain for 0≤j≤n−20\leq j\leq n-2

which is indeed the coefficient of the last member of (5.2)\left(5.2\right) for λ=(n+1)\lambda=\left(n+1\right). In the case m=d⁡((n+1))=(n2)⇔j=n−1m=d\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)=\binom{n}{2}\Leftrightarrow j=n-1 we already know by (3.4)\left(3.4\right) that ⟨qd⁡((n+1))⟩​M(n+1)=1/n!\left\langle q^{d\left(\left(n+1\right)\right)}\right\rangle M_{\left(n+1\right)}=1/n! which is the value given by (5.2)\left(5.2\right). We have therefore proved Theorem 5.1 for λ=(n+1)\lambda=\left(n+1\right).

c) Let us now make an induction on r=l⁡(λ)r=l\left(\lambda\right) with |λ|=n+1\left|\lambda\right|=n+1. The case r=1r=1 is proved by b). Assume that the assertion of Theorem 5.1 is true for all ll such that 1≤l≤r≤n−11\leq l\leq r\leq n-1 and let show that it is true for r+1.r+1. If λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λr,λr+1)\lambda=\left(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},...,\lambda_{r},\lambda_{r+1}\right) with |λ|=n+1\left|\lambda\right|=n+1 and r+1≤nr+1\leq n, (3.10)\left(3.10\right) gives

Mλ=M(λr+1)​Mλ∗+(q−1)​∑i=1rMλ(i)​.M_{\lambda}=M_{\left(\lambda_{r+1}\right)}M_{\lambda^{\ast}}+\left(q-1\right)\sum\limits_{i=1}^{r}M_{\lambda^{\left(i\right)}}\text{.} (5.6)

According to Theorem 3.1, the degree of M(λr+1)​Mλ∗M_{\left(\lambda_{r+1}\right)}M_{\lambda^{\ast}} is

δ=d⁡((λr+1))+d⁡(λ1,λ2,…,λr)=(λr+1−12)+(n+1−λr+1−12)+r−1​,\delta=d\left(\left(\lambda_{r+1}\right)\right)+d\left(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},...,\lambda_{r}\right)=\binom{\lambda_{r+1}-1}{2}+\binom{n+1-\lambda_{r+1}-1}{2}+r-1\text{,}

and (5.1)\left(5.1\right) gives here

v⁡(λ)=v⁡(λ(i))+1​.v\left(\lambda\right)=v\left(\lambda^{\left(i\right)}\right)+1\text{.}

Hence, for mm such that v⁡(λ)≤m≤d⁡(λ)−1v\left(\lambda\right)\leq m\leq d\left(\lambda\right)-1, we have

⟨qm⟩​Mλ​(q)=⟨qm⟩​(q−1)​r​Pn+1(r)​(q)​,\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\lambda}\left(q\right)=\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle\left(q-1\right)rP_{n+1}^{\left(r\right)}\left(q\right)\text{,}

i.e. with (5.2)\left(5.2\right)

⟨qm⟩​Mλ​(q)=r!n!​⟨qm⟩​(q−1)​∑j=0n−1(2​n−r−1−jn−1−j)​qv⁡(λ(i))+j​.\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\lambda}\left(q\right)=\dfrac{r!}{n!}\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle\left(q-1\right)\sum\limits_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{2n-r-1-j}{n-1-j}q^{v\left(\lambda^{\left(i\right)}\right)+j}\text{.} (5.8)

In the right hand side of (5.8)\left(5.8\right), the polynomial after ⟨qm⟩\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle is written by expanding :

−(2​n−r−1n−1)​qv⁡(λ(i))+∑j=1n−1[(2​n−r−1−(j−1)n−1−(j−1))−(2​n−r−1−jn−1−j)]​qv⁡(λ(i))+j\displaystyle-\binom{2n-r-1}{n-1}q^{v\left(\lambda^{\left(i\right)}\right)}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left[\binom{2n-r-1-\left(j-1\right)}{n-1-\left(j-1\right)}-\binom{2n-r-1-j}{n-1-j}\right]q^{v\left(\lambda^{\left(i\right)}\right)+j}
+(2​n−r−1−(n−1)n−1−(n−1))​qv⁡(λ(i))+n​.\displaystyle+\binom{2n-r-1-\left(n-1\right)}{n-1-\left(n-1\right)}q^{v\left(\lambda^{\left(i\right)}\right)+n}\text{.}

With the classical relation (Np)=(N−1p−1)+(N−1p)\binom{N}{p}=\binom{N-1}{p-1}+\binom{N-1}{p}, the square bracket in the above equation becomes :

(2​(n+1)−(r+1)−3−(j−1)n+1−2−(j−1))​.\binom{2\left(n+1\right)-\left(r+1\right)-3-\left(j-1\right)}{n+1-2-\left(j-1\right)}\text{.}

By making the change of index j′=j−1j^{\prime}=j-1 and keeping only the monomials of MλM_{\lambda} with degreee ≥v⁡(λ)\geq v\left(\lambda\right), we obtain for the sum of these monomials

r!n!​∑j′=0n−1(2​(n+1)−(r+1)−3−j′(n+1)−2−j′)​qv⁡(λ)+j′​,\dfrac{r!}{n!}\sum\limits_{j^{\prime}=0}^{n-1}\binom{2\left(n+1\right)-\left(r+1\right)-3-j^{\prime}}{\left(n+1\right)-2-j^{\prime}}q^{v\left(\lambda\right)+j^{\prime}}\text{,}

which is indeed the Pascalian part Pn+1(r+1)P_{n+1}^{\left(r+1\right)} given by (5.2)\left(5.2\right).  

Here is now the proof of the conjectures of Section 4 for part of the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda}, which constitutes the third announced argument.

Corollary 5.2

For any partition λ\lambda such that λ≠1|λ|\lambda\neq 1^{\left|\lambda\right|}, the sequence of the last |λ|−1\left|\lambda\right|-1 coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} is strictly positive and log-concave, then unimodal. If l⁡(λ)<|λ|−1l\left(\lambda\right)<\left|\lambda\right|-1 this sequence is in fact strictly log-concave.

Proof. It is known that the coefficients of the columns of Pascal’s triangle are strictly positif and log-concave. More precisely for any pair of integers (N,p)\left(N,p\right) such that p≥0p\geq 0 et N≥p+1N\geq p+1

(Np)2−(N+1p)​(N−1p)=(N!p!​(N−p)!)2​p​.\binom{N}{p}^{2}-\binom{N+1}{p}\binom{N-1}{p}=\left(\dfrac{N!}{p!\left(N-p\right)!}\right)^{2}p\text{.}

Thus, the columns of Pascal’s triangle are strictly log-concaves for p≥1p\geq 1, the column p=0p=0, consisting of 1, is only log-concave. The corollary follows for JλJ_{\lambda} and λ≠1|λ|\lambda\neq 1^{\left|\lambda\right|} from the proportionality, given by Theorem 5.1 and (3.17)\left(3.17\right), between Pascalian coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} and those of column (n−r−1)\left(n-r-1\right) of Pascal’s triangle.  

Incidentally it is easy to obtain a result similar to Theorem 5.1 for the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} :

Corollary 5.3

For 1≤r≤n−11\leq r\leq n-1, and 0≤i≤n−20\leq i\leq n-2, we have :

⟨q(n−12)−(r−12)−i⟩​Jn(r)=(n−r−1+in−r−1)​,\left\langle q^{\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2}-i}\right\rangle J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=\binom{n-r-1+i}{n-r-1}\text{,} (5.9)

which means that the (n−1)\left(n-1\right) coefficients of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} of the highest degree are given by the first coefficients of column (n−r−1)\left(n-r-1\right) of Pascal’s triangle.

Proof.

Equations (3.13)\left(3.13\right) and (5.2)\left(5.2\right) successively give for n−1≥r≥1n-1\geq r\geq 1, m=d⁡(λ)−im=d\left(\lambda\right)-i and 0≤i≤n−20\leq i\leq n-2 :

⟨qm⟩​q(r2)​Jn(r)r!​(n−r)!=∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r⟨qm⟩​Mλm⁡(λ)!=(r−1)!(n−1)!​(n−r−1+in−r−1)​∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=r1m⁡(λ)!​.\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle q^{\binom{r}{2}}\dfrac{J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}}{r!\left(n-r\right)!}=\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle M_{\lambda}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}=\dfrac{\left(r-1\right)!}{\left(n-1\right)!}\binom{n-r-1+i}{n-r-1}\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{1}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}\text{.}

With (5.5)\left(5.5\right) and after simplification we obtain :

⟨qm⟩​q(r2)​Jn(r)=⟨qm−(r2)⟩​Jn(r)=(n−r−1+in−r−1)​,\left\langle q^{m}\right\rangle q^{\binom{r}{2}}J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=\left\langle q^{m-\binom{r}{2}}\right\rangle J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}=\binom{n-r-1+i}{n-r-1}\text{,}

and (3.3)\left(3.3\right) implies

m−(r2)=(n−12)+r−1−i−(r2)=(n−12)−(r−12)−i​,m-\binom{r}{2}=\binom{n-1}{2}+r-1-i-\binom{r}{2}=\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2}-i\text{,}

which gives (5.9)\left(5.9\right). Moreover, Theorem 6.3 of [8]\left[8\right] shows that (n−12)−(r−12)\binom{n-1}{2}-\binom{r-1}{2} is the degree of Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}, which ends the proof.  

6 To go further

The numerical calculations we performed were implemented on a personal computer. The value n=|λ|=43n=\left|\lambda\right|=43 represents the limit that can be reached within a reasonable computation time. With the three arguments presented, the author has little doubt about the validity of the conjectures (even though, of course, there is no certainty until they have been proven). In any case, the programming codes are available upon request for anyone wishing to use more powerful means to verify these conjectures for a larger integer nn.

The main task now is to prove Conjecture 4.1. Two approaches can be considered for this purpose. The first consists in generalizing the inductive proof from Section 5. Ideally, the goal would be to find a formula that extends the one obtained for Pascalian coefficients so as to include all coefficients. It would already be beneficial to discover a recurrence relation between the JλJ_{\lambda} with coefficients in ℕ⁡[q]\mathbb{N}\left[q\right] - unlike Recurrence (3.18)\left(3.18\right) which has coefficients in ℤ⁡[q]\mathbb{Z}\left[q\right]- in order to prove Conjecture 4.1. The second approach, of a combinatorial nature, would consists in associating to each integer partition λ\lambda, a mathematical object, let’s call it KλK_{\lambda}, whose polynomial JλJ_{\lambda} (or J^λ\widehat{J}_{\lambda}) would be the enumerator of some quantity related to that object. Thus, KλK_{\lambda} would be a generalization of the complete graph KnK_{n} associated with JnJ_{n}, but in a different direction from the contracted graph Kn/rK_{n/r} associated with Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}. It is noteworthy that it seems to emerge from what follows that KλK_{\lambda} cannot be a graph.

Suppose that we have discovered this object KλK_{\lambda}. A fairly natural approach to prove Conjecture 4.2 would then be to reproduce the method used in the proof of Proposition 4.4. This would involve associating to each KλK_{\lambda} a matroid MλM_{\lambda} whose Tutte polynomial would satisfy the following analogue of (4.5)\left(4.5\right) :

J^λ​(q)=Tλ​(1,q)​.\widehat{J}_{\lambda}\left(q\right)=T_{\lambda}\left(1,q\right)\text{.}

Note, in this regard, that the log-concavity of the hh-vector of the independence complex of a matroid has recently been demonstrated for all matroid [2]. This avoids being limited to graphic matroids for ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} (and therefore to graphs for KλK_{\lambda}). However, this approach presents a difficulty. Indeed, we have calculated that :

J(3,2,1)​(q)=10+30​q+35​q2+35​q3+30​q4+20​q5+12​q6+6​q7+2​q8​.J_{\left(3,2,1\right)}\left(q\right)=10+30q+35q^{2}+35q^{3}+30q^{4}+20q^{5}+12q^{6}+6q^{7}+2q^{8}\text{.}

Since the coefficients 22 and 3535 are coprime, J(3,2,1)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)} cannot be reduced to a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. But if we were to find a matroid ℳ\mathcal{M} whose Tutte polynomial TT satisfies J(3,2,1)​(q)=T⁡(1,q)J_{\left(3,2,1\right)}\left(q\right)=T\left(1,q\right), then according to [1, Eq. (1.23) p.138], we would have :

T⁡(1,q)=∑(q−1)|A|−ρ​,T\left(1,q\right)=\sum\left(q-1\right)^{\left|A\right|-\rho}\text{,}

where the sum is taken over all the subsets AA of the ground set EE of ℳ\mathcal{M}, whose ranks are equal to ρ\rho. The highest-degree monomial of T⁡(1,q)T\left(1,q\right) is therefore clearly q|E|−ρq^{\left|E\right|-\rho}, so T⁡(1,q)T\left(1,q\right) would be monic leading to a contradiction.

To put this difficulty into perspective, it is worth noting that the techniques used to prove Huh’s theorem, mentionned in Section 4, have been considerably generalized (see, for example, [6]). It may therefore be conceivable to overcome the difficulty encountered by employing these techniques.

It is worth emphasizing, however, that before embarking on the proof of Conjecture 4.2 on log-concavity, a preliminary step is, as mentionned earlier, to prove Conjecture 4.1 on the strict positivity of the coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda}. The latter poses an interesting challenge from a combinatorial point of view.

I am grateful to Philippe Bodart for the computation of the JλJ_{\lambda} polynomials and the verification of the conjectures up to n=43n=43, using the programs he developped.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
